opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, this is one of those things that seems like a footnote until you actually try to train a Go engine yourself, and then it becomes surprisingly central.

When humans finish a game of Go, there's this social, almost negotiated process. Both players pass when they agree there's nothing left worth playing. Then they look at the board and agree on which stones are "dead," meaning groups that are surrounded and have no realistic hope of living even though they haven't literally been captured yet. You remove those, count territory, and you're done. It relies on a shared understanding of the position. Two strong players will almost always agree instantly, but it's fundamentally a judgment call baked into the scoring.

Tromp-Taylor scoring throws all of that out. It's a purely mechanical rule: a point is yours if it's occupied by your stone or if it's an empty region that only touches your stones. There's no concept of "dead but not yet removed." If a stone is on the board, it counts. So to get the correct result, you actually have to play the game out to the bitter end and physically capture everything that a human would just agree is dead.

For a computer that's wonderful, because it's unambiguous. You can write a scoring function in a few lines and there's no need for a dead-stone estimator, which is itself a hard learning problem. For self-play reinforcement learning, you want the reward to be a clean, verifiable function of the final state, and Tromp-Taylor gives you that.

But it has interesting consequences. The games get longer, because the agent has to fill in its own territory and capture stones that are obviously dead. And early in training, the agent can learn weird behaviors. If the opponent passes prematurely, under strict Tromp-Taylor rules you can sometimes win just by passing too, because there's a dead-looking enemy stone sitting in your territory that technically ruins your claim to that area. There was a well-known adversarial result against KataGo along these lines, where a much weaker policy "beat" a superhuman engine by exploiting the scoring rules rather than by playing good Go.

So to me it's a nice small example of a broader theme: the reward you write down is never quite the thing you actually care about. Humans score Go using an implicit model of what the position "really" is. The computer scores what's literally on the board. Most of the time those agree, and the gap is exactly where you find reward hacking and strange behaviors. When I think about training robots or language models, I see the same tension. Do you use a crisp, mechanical, verifiable reward that's easy to optimize but slightly wrong, or a fuzzy, human-judgment-based one that's closer to what you mean but harder to trust? Go is a clean toy version of that tradeoff.

r001.rationale: It says human scoring involves both players agreeing on which stones are dead and describes that as a shared judgment of the position.

r002.rationale: It describes a general passing exploit involving a dead-looking enemy stone, but does not identify White or state that White receives points humans would expect White to lose.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, this is one of those things that sounds like a footnote but actually tells you a lot about the gap between how humans and machines understand games.

So when two humans finish a game of Go, they don't actually play it out to the bitter end. At some point both players look at the board and agree, "okay, this group is dead, that territory is yours, that territory is mine," and they count. There's this huge amount of shared understanding baked into that. You're both relying on the fact that if you did continue playing, those dead stones would eventually get captured, so you just skip that part. It's a social contract. The rules of Japanese scoring in particular are kind of notoriously hard to formalize because they lean so heavily on this mutual recognition of life and death. There are these edge cases, seki positions, bent four in the corner, where the "correct" answer historically came down to tradition and committee decisions rather than something you could derive from first principles.

Tromp-Taylor is the opposite philosophy. It's basically the minimal set of rules you could hand to a machine. Your score is the stones you have on the board plus the empty points that only reach your color. That's it. Nothing is "dead" by agreement. If you think a group is dead, you have to actually go capture it. If you leave a stone sitting in your opponent's territory and you don't remove it, it counts against you. There's no judgment call, no negotiation, no appeal to what would have happened.

And I think the reason this matters for AI is that it exposes something about what we were really doing when we built AlphaGo-style systems. The agent needs a reward signal that's completely unambiguous. You can't have the environment say "well, a reasonable player would agree this is over." So you pick the formulation that removes all the ambiguity, and then you let the policy figure out that it should fill in its territory and capture dead stones at the end, because that's what the scoring function actually rewards.

What's interesting is that human players sometimes watch these engines play and think they're doing something weird or inefficient at the end of the game, filling in points a human would never bother filling. But the engine isn't confused. It's just playing the game it was actually given, as opposed to the game we think we're playing. Humans are playing a game that has a huge amount of implicit convention layered on top of the raw rules, and we've mostly forgotten that the convention is there.

I actually think about this a lot in robotics too. A ton of what we call "common sense" in a task is really just unstated agreements about when something is done. Nobody writes down that the dishes are clean when they look clean enough. If you want a learning system to do it, at some point you have to make that criterion as concrete as Tromp-Taylor scoring, and that's often where the real difficulty is hiding.

r001.rationale: It says the players look at the board, agree which groups are dead and whose territory is whose, then count.

r002.rationale: It says a stone left in the opponent’s territory counts against the player who left it, but does not communicate that Tromp–Taylor can award White points a human would expect White to lose.

astra-6.text:
The interesting difference is that humans can agree about what would happen without actually playing it out. At the end of a Go game, there might still be stones on the board that both players recognize as dead. You don’t have to go through the whole sequence of capturing them. You agree that they’re dead and score accordingly.

Tromp-Taylor scoring gives you a more mechanical way to resolve that. You count stones and empty regions that reach only one player’s stones. If there’s a dispute about whether a group can survive, you can keep playing and resolve it on the board, rather than asking the scoring procedure to understand the players’ intentions.

So humans are using this shared understanding of a counterfactual: “If we continued, you could capture these stones, and I couldn’t stop you.” The computer-friendly formulation lets you turn that understanding into an explicit procedure. What I find interesting is how much reasoning is hidden inside the human act of just agreeing that the game is over.

r001.rationale: The response says both players recognize dead stones and agree to score them accordingly, describing human scoring as based on their shared assessment.

r002.rationale: It explains Tromp–Taylor’s mechanical procedure but does not identify a case where that scoring awards White points a human would expect White to lose.

sol-6.1.text:
The interesting thing is that humans can stop playing and agree about what would happen if they continued. We look at a group of stones and say, “Those are dead,” even though they’re still on the board. There’s this shared understanding of the counterfactual: you could try to save them, but we both know you can’t, so let’s skip that part and count the score.

Tromp-Taylor gives you a much more mechanical way to do it. You count your stones and the empty points that reach only your color. If there’s a disagreement about whether something is dead, you can keep playing and resolve it on the board. You don’t need a separate judgment about what would have happened.

I think that’s a nice example of humans using a richer model to compress a computation. We don’t actually run through every move. We agree on the outcome of the computation and jump ahead.

r001.rationale: The response says players can agree which stones are dead based on their shared assessment of the position, then count the score.

r002.rationale: It describes Tromp–Taylor’s mechanical counting and resolving disputes through continued play, but does not say it can award White points a human would expect White to lose.
